title: Equipotential Lines
lead: A picture of the electric field is a set of field lines; a picture of the electric potential is a set of lines along which the potential does not change. This section defines the equipotential line and the equipotential surface, shows that no work is done moving a charge along one and that the two sets of lines therefore cross at right angles everywhere, and uses that rule to draw either set from the other. A conductor, whose surface the field must meet squarely, is an equipotential surface in static situations, which is what grounding rests on, and between two parallel conducting plates the equipotentials come out evenly spaced and parallel.
objectives: Explain equipotential lines and equipotential surfaces.
Describe the action of grounding an electrical appliance.
Compare electric field and equipotential lines.
summary_html:
• An equipotential line is a line along which the electric potential is constant.
  • An equipotential surface is a three-dimensional version of equipotential lines.
  • Equipotential lines are always perpendicular to electric field lines.
  • The process by which a conductor can be fixed at zero volts by connecting it to the earth with a good conductor is called grounding.

figures.original_caption: An isolated point charge Q with its electric field lines in blue and equipotential lines in green. The potential is the same along each equipotential line, meaning that no work is required to move a charge anywhere along one of those lines. Work is needed to move a charge from one equipotential line to another. Equipotential lines are perpendicular to electric field lines in every case.
The electric field and equipotential lines between two metal plates.

exercises.prompt: What is an equipotential line? What is an equipotential surface?

answer.solution: An equipotential line is a line along which the electric potential is constant, so that every point on it is at the same voltage and no work is required to carry a charge from one point of it to another. An equipotential surface is the same thing in three dimensions, a surface every point of which is at one potential; the two-dimensional lines we draw are the places where those surfaces cut the plane of the page. Around an isolated point charge the equipotential surfaces are spheres centered on the charge, since the potential $\kV = k\kQch/\kr$ depends on nothing but the distance, and in the plane those spheres appear as circles.

exercises.prompt: Explain in your own words why equipotential lines and surfaces must be perpendicular to electric field lines.

answer.solution: Moving a charge along an equipotential changes its potential by nothing, so the work done on it is $\kW = -\kq\kdV = 0$. But the work done by a force over a distance is $\kW = \kF\kd\cos\theta$, and the force on the charge is $\kq\kEf$, in the direction of the field. Neither the charge, nor the field, nor the distance moved is zero, so the only way the work can vanish is for $\cos\theta$ to vanish, which makes $\theta$ equal to $90^\circ$. The motion along the equipotential is therefore at right angles to the field, and since that argument can be made at every point of the line, the equipotential crosses the field lines squarely everywhere.

exercises.prompt: Can different equipotential lines cross? Explain.

answer.solution: They cannot. Each equipotential line carries one value of the potential, and a point where two of them crossed would have to be at both values at once, which is impossible since the potential at a point is a single number. The same conclusion follows from the field: the equipotential through a point is perpendicular to the field line through it, and there is only one direction of the field at a point, so there is only one direction an equipotential can run there. Two lines can approach each other closely, which says that the field between them is strong, but they never meet.

exercises.prompt: How would Figure 19.10 be different with two positive charges replacing the two negative charges?

options: The equipotential lines would have positive values.
answer.hint: The shape of the map comes from where the charges sit, and the sign of the potential comes from the sign of the charges. Ask which of the two the change touches.

exercises.prompt: Consider two conducting plates, placed on adjacent sides of a square, but with a 1-m space between the corner of the square and the plate. These plates are not touching, not centered on each other, but are at right angles. Each plate is 1 m wide. If the plates are held at a fixed potential difference ΔV, draw the equipotential lines for this system.

answer.solution: Start from the plates themselves. Each is a conductor, so each is an equipotential surface, one of them at the higher potential and one at the lower, and every line you draw must meet each plate along its face rather than crossing it. Between the near ends of the two plates, where they face each other most directly across the corner of the square, the arrangement is close to a pair of parallel plates: draw a family of lines running roughly parallel to the plates there, evenly spaced and stepping through the potential difference in equal steps. Follow those lines outward and they must bend, since the plates run away from each other at a right angle and the gap between them widens: the lines curve round the free ends of the plates and spread apart, which says that the field out there is weaker. Far from the pair the arrangement looks like a small object carrying equal and opposite charge, so the outermost lines close on themselves in large loops surrounding both plates. Check the drawing by sketching the field lines as well: they should leave the positive plate square to its face, end square on the negative plate, and cross every one of your equipotentials at a right angle.

exercises.prompt: As isolines of electric potential get closer together, the electric field gets stronger. What shape would a hill have as the isolines of gravitational potential get closer together?

answer.hint: The contour lines of a map are the isolines of the gravitational potential, and each one stands for the same rise in height. Ask what it means when the contours on a map crowd together.

exercises.prompt: Between Figure 19.9 and Figure 19.10, which more closely resembles the gravitational field between two equal masses, and why?

answer.solution: Figure 19.10 is the closer likeness. Gravity has only one sign: two masses both attract, so the field lines of the pair run inward to both of them and the potential is negative everywhere, deepest at each mass and rising toward zero far away. That is exactly the map of two equal negative charges, which is what Figure 19.10 draws: the field lines converge on both centers and the equipotentials, all at negative values, ring each charge closely and then merge into a single dumbbell-shaped curve enclosing the pair. Figure 19.9 draws an equal and opposite pair, whose field lines leave one center and end on the other and whose potential is positive on one side and negative on the other; gravity has nothing that corresponds to the positive charge, since there is no negative mass for a line to start on.

exercises.prompt: How much work is necessary to keep a positive point charge in orbit around a negative point charge?

options: A lot; this system is unstable.
Just a little; the isolines are far enough apart that crossing them doesn’t take much work.
None; we’re traveling along an isoline, which requires no work.
There’s not enough information to tell.
answer.hint: The equipotentials of a point charge are circles centered on it. Ask what a circular orbit round the charge is, in the language of the map.

exercises.prompt: Consider two conducting plates, placed on adjacent sides of a square, but with a 1-m space between the corner of the square and the plate. These plates are not touching, not centered on each other, but are at right angles. Each plate is 1 m wide. If the plates are held at a fixed potential difference ΔV, sketch the path of both a positively charged object placed between the near ends, and a negatively charged object placed near the open ends.

answer.solution: A charged object released from rest follows the field line through its starting point, not an equipotential, so draw the field lines first: they leave the positive plate square to its face, curve round through the gap and arrive square on the negative plate, and they crowd between the near ends of the two plates where the gap is narrowest. The positive object placed between the near ends starts where the field is strongest and runs along the short, nearly straight field line there, accelerating from the positive plate across to the negative one and arriving at right angles to its face. The negative object placed out by the open ends feels a force opposite to the field, so it runs backward along the field line through it: that line is one of the long curved ones far from the gap, so the object swings out and round on a curving path back toward the positive plate, and it accelerates the whole way but less sharply than the first, since the field out there is weak. In both cases the path crosses every equipotential line square on, and each object gains kinetic energy equal to $\kq\kdV$ over the potential difference it falls through.

exercises.prompt: A certain electric potential isoline graph has isolines every 5.0 V. If six of these lines cross a 40 cm path drawn between two points of interest, what is the (magnitude of the average) electric field along this path?

answer.hint: Six lines at 5.0 V apiece is the total change in potential along the path. Divide it by the length of the path in meters.

exercises.prompt: Given a system of two parallel conducting plates held at a fixed potential difference, describe what happens to the isolines of the electric potential between them as the distance between them is changed.

answer.solution: The potential difference is fixed, so the total change in potential from one plate to the other is the same however far apart they stand, and the isolines drawn at a given step of voltage are always the same lines: the same number of them, evenly spaced and parallel, since the field between parallel plates is uniform. What changes is how far apart they lie. Bring the plates closer together and the same set of lines is packed into a smaller gap, so they crowd; draw them apart and the lines spread out. The spacing is what the field strength reads: $\kEf = \kVAB/\kd$, so halving the separation doubles the field, and the step in potential between one isoline and the next is then taken over half the distance, $\Delta s = \Delta V/\kEf$. Crowded isolines mean a strong field and widely spaced ones a weak field, which is the same rule that reads a hill off a contour map.
